Report writing and documentation
Process design and quality assurance
Domain expertise (for example, building regulations and compliance)

introBlocks.text: Soft skills
Soft skills are personal and interpersonal qualities that enable effective teamwork and leadership. Examples include:

items: Communication (clear, respectful, effective)
Teamwork and collaboration
Empathy and emotional intelligence
Leadership and motivation
Adaptability and flexibility
Conflict resolution
Time management
Creative problem-solving
Decision-making
Integrity and ethical standards

introBlocks.text: Life experience

Not all essential skills can be neatly categorised as hard or soft. Some competencies — such as judgement, resilience, and wisdom — are shaped over time by facing complex situations, making mistakes, learning, and adapting. Life experience provides managers with the ability to see the big picture, connect patterns, and handle the unexpected with calm and insight. For example:

items: Learning from a failed project and applying those lessons to future work
Becoming adaptable after managing diverse teams and encountering cultural challenges
Gaining negotiation skills after years of stakeholder dealings
Developing patience and composure under real-world crisis situations
Learning the value of listening and humility from past leadership errors

introBlocks.text: Often, tasks such as delegating, decision-making, or conflict resolution require both hard and soft skills. For example, effective delegation requires domain knowledge (hard skill) to know what can be delegated, and trust-building (soft skill) to empower others. Similarly, successful time management combines workflow expertise with personal discipline and prioritisation.

sections.title: Mentoring and Coaching

ship.title: Training the next master
body: Every vessel that stayed afloat across generations did so because somebody was taught to hold the helm before the master stepped away from it. Not told about the helm — given it, in fair weather, under supervision, until the hands knew the feel of the ship.
ship.claim: A manager who develops nobody has not built a team; he has built a dependency, and it ends the day he leaves. The measure of your management is not how well the work runs while you are there. It is how well it runs the month you are away.
ship.question: Name the person who could hold your watch tomorrow. If there is no name, that is this module's work.

intro: Every manager in this handbook so far has been treated as someone who gets work done through other people. This section is about the other half of the job, which most managers never formally learn: making those people better than they were when you inherited them.

It is the part of management most easily postponed. Nobody complains this week if you have developed nobody. The costs arrive later, and they arrive as a set of symptoms that look like other problems: you cannot take leave without the work stopping, you cannot promote from within, you are still doing tasks you were doing three years ago, and the same problems come back to you because nobody else has been trained to solve them.
A manager who develops nobody has not built a team. He has built a dependency, and it ends the day he leaves.

blocks.text: These four words are used interchangeably in most organisations and they are not the same thing. They are four stages in a single progression, and the mistake managers make is not choosing the wrong one — it is stopping at the first.

Instructing is showing someone how a task is done and stating the standard it must meet. It is appropriate when the person genuinely does not know, and it is quick. Its limitation is that it develops nothing except the ability to do that task under supervision. A manager who only ever instructs will be instructing the same person on the same task two years from now.

Coaching is helping someone find the answer rather than giving it to them. It is slower than instructing on the first occasion and faster on every occasion afterwards, because what the person acquires is not the answer but the method of reaching it. It is characterised almost entirely by questions.

Mentoring is a longer relationship, less frequent and wider in scope. Coaching is usually about a task or a skill; mentoring is about a person’s development over months and years — their judgement, their reputation, their choices about where they are going. A mentor is often not the person’s line manager, and there are good reasons for that.

Releasing is the point at which you stop. The person holds the responsibility, you are informed rather than consulted, and you read the results rather than supervising the work. Managers find this the hardest of the four, and the difficulty is rarely about the other person’s readiness. It is about what the manager will be if he is no longer needed.
The direction of travel is always towards releasing. A manager still instructing an experienced member of staff after two years has not developed them; he has trained them to wait.

Coaching is a conversation with a particular discipline to it, and the discipline is restraint. The manager who has the answer and is waiting for the other person to reach it will, under time pressure, simply give it — and the moment he does, the conversation stops being coaching and becomes instruction with a longer preamble.
A workable structure for a thirty-minute coaching conversation: Agree what the conversation is about. One sentence, from them, not from you. If they cannot state it, that is the first piece of work.

Establish the situation as they see it. Ask what has been tried and what happened. Do not correct their account at this stage even where you think it is wrong; you are finding out how they are reasoning, and interrupting it tells you nothing.

Open the options. The key question is what else could you do? — asked more than once, past the point of comfort. The first two answers are usually the ones they arrived with. The third and fourth are where coaching earns its time.
Test the options against reality. What would that cost, who would need to agree, what could go wrong. Here you may contribute what you know, because it is information rather than instruction.
Close on a commitment. What will you do, by when, and what will you tell me when it is done. Write it down. A coaching conversation without a dated commitment is a pleasant chat.

Two rules govern the whole of it. The first is that you may not ask a question to which you are visibly waiting for one particular answer; people recognise this immediately and it destroys the exercise. The second is proportion: a useful measure is that the manager should be speaking for less than a third of the conversation.
Mentoring works on a different rhythm — perhaps an hour a month, sustained over a year or more, and concerned with the person rather than the task.

What it covers. Where the person is going and whether their current work is taking them there. Judgement calls they are unsure about. How they are read by others, which is often the single most valuable thing a mentor can tell someone and the thing nobody else will. Choices about training, secondment and promotion.

Why it should usually not be the line manager. A line manager holds the appraisal, the reference and the decision on promotion. There are things a person will not say to somebody holding those. Sound mentoring arrangements pair a person with a manager one or two steps removed, in another department where possible, with an explicit understanding that what is said stays there — subject only to safeguarding and to matters that must be reported.

What the mentor owes. Preparation, kept appointments, candour, and an ending. A mentoring relationship should be reviewed annually and allowed to close without embarrassment when it has done its work.
What the mentee owes. An agenda. A mentee who arrives with nothing has converted the session into a social call, and after three of those the mentor will begin cancelling.
Most development does not happen in a training room. It happens because a manager deliberately gave somebody work slightly beyond what they had done before, and stayed close enough to catch a fall.

The practical methods, in rough order of cost: Extending the task. Give the same work with one new element attached — the analysis as well as the data, the recommendation as well as the options, the presentation as well as the paper.

Deputising. Send someone in your place, properly briefed, with the authority to speak. This is the single most effective development method available to a manager and the one most often withheld, usually on the grounds that the meeting is too important — which is precisely why it develops anybody.
Shadowing and reverse shadowing. They watch you do it; then you watch them do it and say nothing until afterwards. The second half is the part that gets skipped.
Project ownership. A discrete piece of work with a beginning, an end and a name attached to it. Small and finished beats large and abandoned.

Structured stretch with a safety net. Say plainly: this is beyond what you have done, I expect it to be uncomfortable, here is what I will catch. People take on far more when the terms are stated honestly than when they are told it will be fine.

The manager’s obligation in all of this is to protect the person from the consequences of a development failure that he chose to expose them to. A manager who delegates a stretch task and then disowns the result in front of others will not be trusted with anybody’s development again, and word travels faster than he expects.
Development that is not written down does not happen; it is displaced by whatever is urgent. A workable plan for one person fits on a single page and contains five things:

items: Where they are now — stated plainly, agreed by both, including the uncomfortable part.
Where they are going — the next role or the next level of responsibility, named. “General improvement” is not a destination.
The two or three gaps — no more. A plan with nine development areas is a plan nobody will act on.
What will be done about each — the specific task, deputising opportunity, course or mentoring arrangement, with a date.
When it will be reviewed — quarterly, in the diary now, not “when we get a chance”.

blocks.text: Review it in the meeting you have already scheduled rather than creating a new one. The commonest cause of a dead development plan is that it was owned by an event that never recurred.

tests: Can I name a person who could hold my responsibilities for a month if I were unavailable tomorrow?
Has anyone been promoted out of my team in the last two years?
When I last explained something to a team member, did I ask or did I tell?
Do I have a written development plan for each person I manage — or for any of them?
When did I last send someone to a meeting in my place?
Am I still personally doing a task I was doing three years ago that somebody else could now do?
Do I know what each of my staff wants to be doing in three years?
Have I ever told a team member honestly how they are perceived by others?
When a stretch task I assigned went wrong, did I defend the person publicly?
Of the four stages — instructing, coaching, mentoring, releasing — which am I stuck at, and with whom?
questions: Who in this organisation was developed here rather than recruited already formed? What did that take, and who did it?
Why do managers here avoid deputising? Name the real reason rather than the stated one.
Should a mentor be someone’s line manager? What is currently possible in an organisation of our size?
What happens here to a person who takes on a stretch task and fails at it? What does the answer teach everybody watching?
Is developing people assessed in anybody’s appraisal here? If not, why would anyone prioritise it?
review.exercise: Choose one person you manage. Write their one-page development plan: where they are now, where they are going, the two or three gaps, what will be done about each with dates, and a review date entered in your diary before you leave the room. Then hold the conversation — and let them change the plan.

items: Delegate a real task through the four steps — select, brief, authorise, follow up — and state the difference between delegating and dumping.
Name the conditions that must exist before delegation is possible, and which of them is currently missing in their team.
Make and record a decision using a stated method, distinguishing decisions that need consultation from those that do not.
Audit a week of their own time and identify the work that only they could have done.
Run a meeting with a purpose, a paper and a decision, and close it with named actions and dates.
Complete an honest self-appraisal and name one hidden quality they need to develop.
Distinguish instructing, coaching, mentoring and releasing, and identify which stage each of their team members is at.
Hold a coaching conversation using open questions rather than instruction, and set a development objective for one person.
outcomes.evidence: one task genuinely delegated with a written brief, a time audit, a self-appraisal, and one written development plan for a named team member.

modules.title: Solving and Improving
modules.tagline: Leaks, storms, and knowing your own vessel

verses.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ
verses.text: Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.
Tie her, and trust in Allah.” — said to a man who left his camel untied and said he was relying on Allah.
verses.ref: Narrated by Anas ibn Mālik — Sunan al-Tirmidhī 2517

why: This module is about diagnosis and change, and both texts refuse the same excuse. The verse places the starting point of any improvement inside the team, not in the circumstances it complains about. The ḥadīth settles the question every risk register really asks: reliance on Allah is not an alternative to taking the precaution — it comes after it. A manager who has not tied the camel is not practising tawakkul, only optimism.

sections.title: Problem Solving

ship.title: The leak below the waterline
body: Problems at sea come in two kinds. There is the storm you can see, which frightens everybody and is usually survivable, and there is the slow leak below the waterline, which frightens nobody until the ship is low in the water. Most organisational failures are leaks, not storms.
ship.claim: The seven-step diagnostic in this section is a sounding: it makes you go compartment by compartment instead of standing on deck deciding which part of the weather to blame.
ship.question: The last thing that went badly — was it a storm or a leak? If you called it a storm, check again.

intro: Problems are inevitable in any organisation. How managers and leaders respond to problems determines organisational success, team morale, and long-term viability. Problem-solving is not a single skill but an integrated approach combining analysis, creativity, emotional intelligence, and wisdom. This section explores problem-solving methodology, how organisations learn from failures, the importance of development and change management, and common administrative challenges managers face.

Effective problem-solving follows a structured approach, though the process must remain flexible enough to adapt to different problem types. Problems range from routine operational issues (a piece of equipment malfunctions) to complex systemic challenges (declining productivity across multiple departments) to unprecedented crises (sudden market disruption, natural disasters). While the process may vary slightly, a fundamental methodology provides the foundation for effective problem-solving.

Many organisations fail at this crucial first step by jumping to solutions without truly understanding the problem. Defining the problem clearly requires asking: What exactly is happening? When did it start? How widespread is it? Who is affected? What is the impact? What do we know versus what do we assume? Managers should gather data and evidence rather than relying on intuition or first impressions. For example, if customer satisfaction scores are declining, the problem is not “poor customer service” (a vague diagnosis) but rather “response time to customer enquiries increased from two hours to eight hours over the past three months, correlated with the departure of two customer service representatives” (a clear, specific problem). Clear problem definition prevents wasted effort on addressing symptoms rather than root causes.

Once the problem is clearly defined, the next step is determining why it exists. This requires moving beyond surface symptoms. The “5 Whys” technique is useful: ask “Why?” repeatedly until you reach the true root cause.
For example:

This analysis reveals that the true root cause is not that pupils are choosing to stay at home, but that the school has no mechanism for noticing and acting on a pupil falling behind. Addressing the symptom (telephoning parents about attendance) without addressing the root cause (undetected learning gaps) would likely result in the same problem recurring next term with a different group.
Root causes typically fall into several categories that suggest different solutions:

Once root causes are understood, the next step is generating potential solutions. This is where creativity is essential. Many problems have multiple valid solutions, and the best solution often emerges from considering multiple approaches. During this brainstorming phase, withhold judgement and generate a wide range of possibilities before evaluating them. Involve people with different perspectives — those closest to the problem often have valuable insights that senior managers miss. For example, if the problem is declining quality in a manufacturing process, involve quality inspectors, machine operators, maintenance staff, and supervisors in generating solutions. They collectively may identify that inadequate maintenance, operator training gaps, and changes in supplier materials are all contributing. Potential solutions might include: an increased maintenance schedule, a retraining programme, changing suppliers, modifying machine settings, or a combination of approaches.
Solutions should be evaluated against multiple criteria to identify the best option:

Once the best solution is selected, development and implementation planning is crucial. This should include clear objectives and success metrics, a detailed action plan with timeline and milestones, assignment of responsibilities and accountability, resource requirements and allocation, a communication strategy to ensure stakeholder understanding, risk mitigation plans, and contingency approaches. Many good solutions fail due to poor implementation, not because the solution itself was flawed. Assign an owner responsible for the solution’s implementation. Establish check-in points to monitor progress. Be prepared to adjust the implementation plan if circumstances change or if early results suggest modifications are needed.

After implementation, ongoing monitoring determines whether the solution actually solved the problem or if adjustment is needed. Define specific metrics that indicate whether the solution is working. Collect data regularly. Compare actual results against expected results. Were the intended outcomes achieved? Were there unexpected consequences? Is the problem actually resolved or only partially addressed? Schedule formal evaluation points — perhaps 30, 90, and 180 days after implementation — to assess effectiveness. This phase is critical for both validating solutions and extracting lessons for future problem-solving. Organisations that skip this step miss crucial learning opportunities.

blocks.text: Organisations that excel at problem-solving treat failures not as events to hide or punish, but as learning opportunities. Unfortunately, many organisations suppress failure reporting, which means problems are discovered too late, lessons are not extracted, and the same mistakes repeat. Building a culture where failures become learning opportunities is essential for organisational growth.
Why learning from failure matters:

items: Prevents repetition of mistakes across the organisation
Accelerates improvement by learning from collective experience
Builds resilience — organisations that fail small, learn, and adapt survive better than those that avoid all risk
Attracts innovative thinking — people are more willing to propose creative ideas if failure is not punished
Reduces defensive behaviour — when people fear blame, they hide problems rather than surfacing them for collective solving
Creates psychological safety — team members take reasonable risks and speak up about issues

blocks.text: Learning does not have to be paid for first-hand. A near-miss or failure at another organisation — reported in the press, discussed at a sector network, or shared informally by a peer manager — carries the same lesson at none of the cost. Managers who make a habit of asking “what happened there, and could it happen here?” catch risks their own organisation has not yet experienced.
Creating a blame-free problem analysis culture

When a problem or failure occurs, the instinct in many organisations is to find who to blame and punish them. This approach has catastrophic consequences: people hide problems, errors compound, and the organisation never learns. Instead, organisations should implement “blameless post-mortem” processes when significant problems occur. This means analysing what happened and why without focus on individual blame. The questions asked are: What were the conditions that led to this outcome? What systems, processes, or decisions contributed? What can we learn? How do we prevent similar situations? Who do we need to support? This approach acknowledges that most problems result from systemic issues or poor processes, not individual negligence. It also creates safety for people to report problems early rather than hiding them.
The post-mortem process:

items: Timeliness: conduct the analysis soon after the event while details are fresh
Participation: include people involved in the situation and those with relevant expertise
Psychological safety: explicitly state that the purpose is learning, not blame
Chronological review: walk through what happened step by step based on evidence
Contributing factors: identify all factors that contributed — technological, human, systemic, environmental
Root causes: analyse why these factors existed rather than stopping at surface causes
Learning points: extract specific lessons — what can we learn from this?
Action items: identify specific changes to prevent recurrence — what will we do differently?
Documentation: record findings so the organisation can reference them and avoid repetition
Follow-up: track that agreed changes are actually implemented

blocks.text: Organisational learning practices
Beyond individual post-mortems, organisations can systematise learning through:

items: Regular retrospectives — monthly or quarterly reflection on what worked and what didn’t
Lessons learned documentation — maintaining a searchable database of past problems, solutions, and outcomes
Cross-functional learning sessions — teams sharing what they’ve learned with other departments
Case studies — documenting significant challenges, how they were addressed, and results
Expert interviews — capturing wisdom from experienced managers and staff
Trend analysis — identifying patterns across multiple problems to address systemic issues
Mentoring — experienced employees sharing lessons with newer or less experienced team members

blocks.title: learning from failure
blocks.text: A centre runs a distribution of winter supplies and it goes badly. Families queue for four hours, some are turned away after being told to come, and two households on the list receive nothing at all. The easy response is to blame the volunteer who was managing the queue. Instead the manager sits down with everyone involved the following morning and asks what happened, making it clear at the outset that he is looking for the fault in the arrangements and not for a person to punish. Four things come out. The list was drawn up three weeks earlier and never updated, so some families had already moved. Nobody had been given the job of checking arrivals against the list, so it was done by whoever was free. The supplies arrived an hour late because no one had confirmed the delivery the night before. And two volunteers who had spotted the queue building said nothing, because they assumed someone senior already knew. Each of these is a gap in the arrangements, not a failure of character. Four changes follow: lists are verified in the week of a distribution, one named person owns the check-in desk, deliveries are confirmed the previous evening, and any volunteer who sees a problem forming is expected to say so directly to the person in charge. The next distribution takes half the time. This is the difference between a post-mortem and a search for someone to blame: the first produces four changes, the second produces one resignation and the same failure next winter.

Organisations must continuously evolve to remain effective. Markets change, regulations shift, technologies emerge, team composition changes, and organisational scale increases. Problem-solving is sometimes tactical — solving today’s specific problem. But organisations also need strategic development: planned change that improves organisational capacity and performance. Understanding when change is needed and how to implement it effectively is a critical leadership competency.
Types of organisational change
Incremental change

Incremental change is ongoing improvement within existing systems and structures. Examples include improving a process slightly, upgrading equipment, expanding a successful programme, or adding team members. Incremental change is typically less disruptive, requires lower investment, and can often be implemented quickly.
However, incremental change alone is insufficient when organisations face fundamental shifts. Incremental improvements to a typewriter business would not have prepared it for the digital revolution.
Transformational change

Transformational change fundamentally alters how the organisation operates — shifting operating models, restructuring operations, entering new markets, or adopting entirely new approaches. Examples include moving from in-person to remote operations, transitioning from a centralised to a distributed organisational structure, adopting new technology platforms, or redefining the organisational mission. Transformational change is more disruptive, requires significant investment and effort, and carries higher risk. But it is sometimes necessary for organisational survival and relevance. Organisations that resist needed transformational change eventually become obsolete.
When development or change is needed
Managers and leaders should recognise signals that development and change are needed:

items: Market or industry shifts: customer needs change, new competitors emerge, technology disrupts, the regulatory environment shifts. Organisations must adapt or lose relevance.
Internal performance issues: despite problem-solving efforts, underlying performance gaps persist. This may indicate that minor adjustments are insufficient and deeper change is needed.
Capacity constraints: current systems or structures cannot support organisational growth or new objectives.
Scaling requires development.
Talent and culture issues: high turnover, disengagement, or culture misalignment may signal that organisational structures, leadership approaches, or work systems need redesign.
Financial pressure: declining revenue or sustainability requires strategic reassessment and organisational development.
Strategic opportunities: new opportunities become available that require organisational expansion, new capabilities, or structural adaptation.
Team feedback and input: staff, beneficiaries, or stakeholders express that current approaches are insufficient or outdated.

blocks.text: The change management process

Implementing organisational change successfully requires a structured approach. Many change initiatives fail not because the change direction is wrong, but because the change process is poorly managed.
Phase 1: Build the case for change

Before implementing change, leaders must build understanding of why change is needed. This involves (1) analysing the current state — what is working and what is not, (2) envisioning the future state — what will be better after change, (3) identifying the gap — what needs to change to move from current to future state, and (4) articulating the urgency — why this change is needed now, not later. This case for change should be communicated clearly and repeatedly so that team members understand the “why” behind the change. Without understanding why, people resist change as unnecessary disruption.
Phase 2: Engage and involve stakeholders

Change is more likely to succeed when those affected by the change are involved in shaping it. This means (1) identifying key stakeholders who will be impacted, (2) involving them in problem diagnosis and solution design, (3) seeking their input on implementation approaches, and (4) addressing their concerns and fears openly. Involvement creates both better solutions (stakeholders have valuable knowledge) and higher buy-in (people support changes they helped shape). Organisations that impose change from the top without stakeholder involvement face resistance, resentment, and lower success rates.
Phase 3: Communicate clearly and repeatedly

Communication is critical throughout change. Messages should include what is changing and why, how it affects different groups, the timeline and milestones, what support is available, and what success looks like. Communication should happen repeatedly through multiple channels — town halls, written updates, team meetings, one-to-ones. Expect that people will need to hear the message many times before it registers. Also create channels for questions and concerns; two-way communication is essential. Address misinformation and rumours promptly.
Phase 4: Provide support and remove barriers

Change often requires people to learn new skills, adjust to new processes, or adapt to new structures. Provide (1) training and coaching, (2) resources and tools needed for the change, (3) time to learn and adjust, (4) mentoring and support, and (5) removal of obstacles blocking change implementation. Monitor how people are adjusting and provide additional support where needed. Change is harder for some people than others — individualised support acknowledges this reality.
Phase 5: Monitor and course-correct

After implementation, track whether the change is achieving intended results. Collect data on key metrics. Gather feedback on what is working and what is not. Be prepared to adjust the change if it is not working as expected or if unintended consequences emerge. Change is not a one-time event but an ongoing process of implementation, learning, and adjustment. Organisations that remain rigid after initial implementation miss opportunities for improvement.

Practical example — organisational development: An organisation begins with one centre and grows to four across the governorate. The structure that worked for one no longer works for four. Every decision — a repair, a new class, a replacement trainer — still travels to the head office and waits there, and centre supervisors have begun to describe themselves as caretakers rather than managers. Leadership recognises this as a structural problem rather than a discipline problem, and the answer is to move authority closer to the work. Rather than announcing a new structure, they do six things. They ask each centre what decisions it is currently waiting on and how long the wait is. They involve the supervisors in designing what the new arrangement should be. They set a transition period of six months rather than a single changeover date. They train supervisors in the areas they will now decide on — small budgets, timetabling, local hiring — and state the limits in writing. They establish a monthly meeting of all four supervisors so the centres do not drift apart. And they track three things: how long a decision now takes, whether supervisors are using the authority given to them, and whether standards have held. After six months decisions are faster, supervisors are managing rather than relaying, and the head office is doing the work only it can do.

Six problems account for most of what goes wrong administratively. They are set out below with the form each one takes, the cause that usually sits underneath it, and the first correction to make. The pattern is consistent: the visible symptom is rarely the fault.

blocks.caption: Six common administrative problems
head: Problem
How it shows itself
What usually causes it
First correction
rows: Decisions do not reach the people affected; rumour fills the gap
No defined channel, or too many; one announcement treated as enough
Name the channel for each type of message, and a person who owns it
Work duplicates; critical tasks fall between people
Job descriptions absent, vague or overtaken by growth
Map every function to a named owner; write it down and circulate it
Work takes longer than it should; everyone does it differently
Processes grew informally and were never designed or recorded
Map what actually happens, remove needless approvals, document it
Standards are not met and nothing follows; the willing carry the rest
No measurable expectations, no regular feedback, hard conversations avoided
Set measurable goals per role and give feedback monthly, not annually
Persistent overtime, falling quality, rising turnover
Scope added without anything removed; poor prioritisation
Review the workload before the headcount; stop or defer lower-priority work
New systems adopted in name; old practice continues
The reason was never explained and those affected were never consulted
Explain why before what, involve the people affected, pilot before rolling out

blocks.text: Each of these has the same shape. Something was never made explicit — a channel, a role, a process, a standard, a limit, a reason — and people filled the gap with assumption. The correction in every case is to make the implicit thing explicit and then hold it.

blocks.title: several problems at once
blocks.text: A charity faces high turnover, inconsistent service quality and repeated missed deadlines. These look like three problems. Investigation shows one: nobody had written down who was responsible for what after the organisation doubled in size. Staff were unclear about expectations, so quality varied; work fell between roles, so deadlines slipped; people felt unsupported, so they left. The remedy was a role-mapping exercise, written job descriptions, and a monthly one-to-one for every member of staff. Turnover fell within two quarters. Treating the three symptoms separately would have addressed none of them.

subsections.title: When Results Are Unsatisfactory: A Seven-Step Diagnostic

blocks.text: The problem-solving method above starts from a specific problem. Sometimes there is no specific problem — results are simply not what they should be, and it is not obvious why. In that situation a sequenced review of the organisation itself is more useful than analysing any single failure.

blocks.alt: When results are unsatisfactory, work down in order: clarify the desired result, determine the essential activities, design the structure, develop the management, delegate the supervision, train the people, simplify the procedures

blocks.text: Work through these seven steps in order, because a fault at an earlier step makes everything below it ineffective. Training people to follow a procedure that serves the wrong objective produces nothing except better-executed waste.

items: Clarify the desired result. What are we actually trying to achieve, and is that shared?

blocks.text: Disagreement here explains more poor performance than any other single cause, and it is rarely visible until someone asks.

items: Determine the essential activities. Which activities genuinely contribute to that result? Most organisations accumulate work that once had a purpose and no longer does. Establish what is essential before organising around it.
Design the structure. Does the way work is grouped and reported fit the activities that matter? A structure built for what the organisation used to do will obstruct what it now does.
Develop the management. Are the people leading this work equipped to lead it? A capable structure staffed by managers who have never been developed will underperform indefinitely.
Delegate the supervision. Has authority been passed down alongside responsibility? People held accountable for results they cannot influence will disengage.
Train the people. Do those doing the work know how to do it? Only at this point does individual capability become the limiting factor.
Simplify the procedures. Are the methods themselves the obstacle? Simplification is genuinely valuable — but it is the last step, not the first.

blocks.text: Why the order matters. Most managers begin at step seven, because procedures are the easiest thing to change and changing them feels productive. Most underperformance originates in steps one to three, where change is slower, more political, and more uncomfortable. A team that has streamlined its procedures four times in three years is usually telling you that the real problem is somewhere near the top of this list.
None of this produces improvement on its own. There is no improvement except through change, and each of these steps identifies a change that someone must decide to make.

Organisations that excel at problem-solving, learning from failures, implementing necessary change, and addressing common administrative challenges develop organisational capabilities that enable sustained success. Managers who master problem-solving frameworks, who create psychological safety for honest problem identification, who remain curious about root causes rather than jumping to solutions, and who involve others in both diagnosing and solving problems build high-performing organisations. Problem-solving is not a discrete event but an ongoing organisational capability. Organisations that view problems as opportunities to learn and improve, rather than as failures to hide, continuously strengthen their performance and adaptability. In a rapidly changing world, the ability to solve problems effectively is perhaps the most valuable organisational capability.

tests: When a problem lands, do I define it in specific terms before proposing solutions?
Do I distinguish the symptom from the cause, in writing?
Have I applied the “5 Whys” to a real problem in the last month?
Do I involve the people closest to the work in generating solutions?
Do I evaluate more than one option before choosing?
Does every solution I implement have a named owner and a review date?
Do I schedule evaluation points, or assume the fix worked?
Has anyone in my team reported a failure to me recently? If not, why not?
Do we document lessons anywhere another team could actually find them?
When change is needed, do I build the case before announcing the decision?
questions: Name a problem we have solved more than once. Why did it come back?
Is it safe to report a failure here? What is the evidence either way?
Which of the six common administrative problems is most alive in our organisation right now?
When we last changed something significant, which of the five change phases did we skip?
Who in our organisation holds knowledge we would lose tomorrow if they left?
review.exercise: Choose a recurring problem in your area and work it through the “5 Whys” on paper. Note whether the root cause you reach is within your authority to fix. If it is not, identify who must be involved and arrange to speak to them.

introBlocks.text: Problems are inevitable in any organisation. How managers and leaders respond to problems determines organisational success, team morale, and long-term viability. Problem-solving is not a single skill but an integrated approach combining analysis, creativity, emotional intelligence, and wisdom. This section explores problem-solving methodology, how organisations learn from failures, the importance of development and change management, and common administrative challenges managers face.
Problem-solving framework and methodology

Effective problem-solving follows a structured approach, though the process must remain flexible enough to adapt to different problem types. Problems range from routine operational issues (a piece of equipment malfunctions) to complex systemic challenges (declining productivity across multiple departments) to unprecedented crises (sudden market disruption, natural disasters). While the process may vary slightly, a fundamental methodology provides the foundation for effective problem-solving.
Step 1: Define the problem clearly

Many organisations fail at this crucial first step by jumping to solutions without truly understanding the problem. Defining the problem clearly requires asking: What exactly is happening? When did it start? How widespread is it? Who is affected? What is the impact? What do we know versus what do we assume? Managers should gather data and evidence rather than relying on intuition or first impressions. For example, if customer satisfaction scores are declining, the problem is not “poor customer service” (a vague diagnosis) but rather “response time to customer enquiries increased from two hours to eight hours over the past three months, correlated with the departure of two customer service representatives” (a clear, specific problem). Clear problem definition prevents wasted effort on addressing symptoms rather than root causes.
Step 2: Analyse root causes

Once the problem is clearly defined, the next step is determining why it exists. This requires moving beyond surface symptoms. The “5 Whys” technique is useful: ask “Why?” repeatedly until you reach the true root cause.
For example:

items: Symptom: pupil attendance in Year 9 has fallen from 94 per cent to 81 per cent over one term
Why 1: a group of pupils is regularly absent on the same two days each week
Why 2: those days carry the lessons the pupils find hardest to follow
Why 3: the pupils fell behind in those subjects last year and were never brought back up
Why 4: the school has no way of identifying a pupil who has fallen behind until the end-of-year examination
Why 5: the school’s assessment system records marks but nobody is responsible for acting on a falling pattern

introBlocks.text: This analysis reveals that the true root cause is not that pupils are choosing to stay at home, but that the school has no mechanism for noticing and acting on a pupil falling behind. Addressing the symptom (telephoning parents about attendance) without addressing the root cause (undetected learning gaps) would likely result in the same problem recurring next term with a different group.
Understanding root cause categories
Root causes typically fall into several categories that suggest different solutions:

introBlocks.caption: Root cause categories
head: Category
What it looks like
Kind of solution it points to
rows: The task is beyond current training, experience or capacity
Training, coaching, recruitment or redistributing work
The steps themselves are missing, unclear or in the wrong order
Equipment, software or records do not support the work
Repair, replace or introduce a system
Not enough time, money, people or materials for what is asked
People do not know what is expected or what is happening
Define channels, owners and feedback loops
Nobody owns the decision, or the wrong level holds it
Clarify roles, reporting lines and delegated authority

introBlocks.text: Step 3: Identify potential solutions

Once root causes are understood, the next step is generating potential solutions. This is where creativity is essential. Many problems have multiple valid solutions, and the best solution often emerges from considering multiple approaches. During this brainstorming phase, withhold judgement and generate a wide range of possibilities before evaluating them. Involve people with different perspectives — those closest to the problem often have valuable insights that senior managers miss. For example, if the problem is declining quality in a manufacturing process, involve quality inspectors, machine operators, maintenance staff, and supervisors in generating solutions. They collectively may identify that inadequate maintenance, operator training gaps, and changes in supplier materials are all contributing. Potential solutions might include: an increased maintenance schedule, a retraining programme, changing suppliers, modifying machine settings, or a combination of approaches.
Solution evaluation criteria
Solutions should be evaluated against multiple criteria to identify the best option:

items: Effectiveness: will it actually solve the root cause? How thoroughly does it address the problem?
Cost: what is the financial investment required? Is it within budget?
Timeline: how quickly can it be implemented? Does the timeline match organisational urgency?
Risk: what could go wrong? Are there unintended consequences?
Feasibility: is it practical to implement given current capabilities and constraints?
Sustainability: will it create a lasting solution or is it temporary?
Alignment: does it align with organisational strategy, values, and culture?
Buy-in: will key stakeholders support this solution?

introBlocks.text: Step 4: Develop and implement the solution

Once the best solution is selected, development and implementation planning is crucial. This should include clear objectives and success metrics, a detailed action plan with timeline and milestones, assignment of responsibilities and accountability, resource requirements and allocation, a communication strategy to ensure stakeholder understanding, risk mitigation plans, and contingency approaches. Many good solutions fail due to poor implementation, not because the solution itself was flawed. Assign an owner responsible for the solution’s implementation. Establish check-in points to monitor progress. Be prepared to adjust the implementation plan if circumstances change or if early results suggest modifications are needed.
Step 5: Monitor, evaluate, and learn

After implementation, ongoing monitoring determines whether the solution actually solved the problem or if adjustment is needed. Define specific metrics that indicate whether the solution is working. Collect data regularly. Compare actual results against expected results. Were the intended outcomes achieved? Were there unexpected consequences? Is the problem actually resolved or only partially addressed? Schedule formal evaluation points — perhaps 30, 90, and 180 days after implementation — to assess effectiveness. This phase is critical for both validating solutions and extracting lessons for future problem-solving. Organisations that skip this step miss crucial learning opportunities.

introBlocks.title: the problem-solving process
introBlocks.text: A training centre finds that classes are starting late almost every day. The obvious assumption is that trainers are unpunctual. Before acting on it, the manager spends a week simply watching what happens at the start of each session. Three causes appear, none of them the assumed one. The store cupboard holding projectors and handouts is locked, and only one member of staff has the key. Two classrooms are timetabled back to back with no gap, so the room is still occupied when the next group arrives. And registration is done on paper at the door, which takes six or seven minutes with a full class. Three small changes follow: a second key is cut and held at reception, a fifteen-minute gap is built between sessions in those two rooms, and the register is passed round during the first activity instead of at the door. Within a month, classes start on time. Had the manager acted on the first assumption, he would have reprimanded trainers who were not at fault, and the classes would still have started late.

sections.title: Types of Organisations

ship.title: Different vessels, different waters
body: A fishing boat, a ferry, a cargo ship and a lifeboat are all vessels, and almost nothing about running one transfers cleanly to another. Purpose, scale and structure decide what good management looks like here, and borrowing another organisation's practice without asking what kind of vessel it was built for is how sound ideas sink good teams.
ship.claim: Scale is the one that catches people. The boat that handles perfectly with a crew of six needs a different watch system at twenty, and the master who does not change the system blames the crew.
ship.question: If your organisation doubled in twelve months, name the first thing that would break. That is the thing to build now.

intro: The approach that works in one organisational context can fail in another. A manager who understands what kind of organisation they work in — and what that implies for how decisions get made and what counts as success — adapts faster than one who applies a single method everywhere. This section is deliberately brief: its purpose is to help you locate your own organisation, not to survey the field.

blocks.text: For-profit commercial organisations exist primarily to generate profit for owners or shareholders. Profit is the measure of success, returned to owners or reinvested for growth.
They compete in markets and must balance profitability against long-term sustainability.

Non-profit organisations exist to serve a mission rather than to generate profit. Revenues are reinvested in the mission rather than distributed. They operate across education, healthcare, humanitarian aid, social services, conservation and the arts. Despite the name, they must still achieve financial sustainability to continue operating.
Government and public sector organisations serve the public interest and deliver services mandated by law. They are funded largely from taxation and accountable to elected officials and the public.

Social enterprises sit between the first two. Their primary purpose is social or environmental impact, but they earn revenue through trading and operate with commercial discipline. They demonstrate that earned income and mission need not conflict — indeed, trading income can be what makes mission-driven work financially sustainable.
Size affects structure, management approach, culture and capability more than most managers expect. A team of five operates in a fundamentally different way from an organisation of a thousand.

Small (5–50 people). Managers can see the whole operation. Communication is direct and frequent, decision-making usually centralised with the founder or leader. The challenge is preserving that energy and cohesion while building enough system to allow growth. Organisations that formalise too early slow themselves down; those that never formalise hit a ceiling where the absence of systems prevents further growth.

Medium (50–500 people). The critical transition. Not everyone hears the same message directly any more. Middle managers become essential but may have had no management training. Culture shifts as the organisation grows. Success here depends on clarifying mission, establishing communication channels, developing middle management capability, and building systems that enable rather than constrain. Organisations that navigate this transition keep growing; those that don’t stall.

Large (500+ people). Managers oversee functional areas rather than whole operations, and must work within formal systems. Informal communication no longer reaches everyone. The central risk is bureaucracy that stifles responsiveness. Effective managers here understand both the formal structure and the informal networks through which work actually happens, and mid-level managers carry the load of translating strategy downwards and surfacing reality upwards.

Beyond type and size, how an organisation is arranged shapes how it is managed. Hierarchical structures organise around function or geography and give clear authority lines at the cost of speed. Matrix structures overlay two hierarchies — typically function and project — which improves resource sharing but creates competing demands on the same people. Distributed structures minimise hierarchical levels, moving decisions closer to the work at the cost of consistency. No model is correct in the abstract; each trades something away.

tests: Can I describe my organisation by ownership, purpose, size, and structure?
Do I know what counts as success here, in terms our funders and beneficiaries would recognise?
Am I applying an approach learned in a different type of organisation without adjusting it?
Do our incentives reward mission achievement or simply activity?
At our current size, are our systems ahead of our growth or behind it?
Which of our processes were designed for an organisation smaller than we now are?
Do I understand the informal networks here as well as the formal chart?
Where does our structure slow decisions without improving them?
Do local or field teams have the autonomy their context requires?
If we doubled in size next year, what would break first?
questions: Which scale band are we in, and which transition are we facing next?
Where does the commercial playbook fail in our setting, and where does it still apply?
What actually motivates people here, and do our systems reflect it?
Are we more centralised or more distributed than our work requires?
What would we have to give up in order to grow, and is it worth it?
review.exercise: Write down the three systems that would break first if your organisation doubled in size. Rank them by how long each would take to fix, and start with the slowest.

items: Apply a structured problem-solving sequence to a real problem rather than moving straight to a remedy.
Distinguish a symptom from a cause, and a storm from a slow leak.
Conduct a review of a failure that produces a lesson and a change, without producing a culprit.
Recognise the six common administrative problems in their own area and name which is most present.
Work through the seven-step diagnostic when results are unsatisfactory, and reach a conclusion supported by evidence.
Explain why people resist change, and plan an introduction of a change that addresses the reason rather than overriding it.
Describe their own organisation by purpose, scale and structure, and name the first thing that would break if it doubled in size.
outcomes.evidence: one completed seven-step diagnostic on a live problem, one written failure review, and a one-page organisational description with a stated growth risk.

modules.title: The Systems That Hold It Together
modules.tagline: Watches, standing orders and the ship’s log

verses.ar: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا تَدَايَنتُم بِدَيْنٍ إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى فَاكْتُبُوهُ
verses.text: O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.
Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account.
verses.ref: A saying of ‘Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, not a prophetic ḥadīth — reported by al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Abī Shaybah

why: The longest verse in the Qur’an is about record-keeping between people who trust each other — which is the entire argument of this module. Documentation is not distrust; it is what protects trust from memory. ‘Umar’s instruction is the internal control: an organisation that audits itself before the regulator, the donor or the trustees do so is one that still has time to put things right.

sections.title: Administrative Discipline

ship.title: The watch and the bell
body: Discipline aboard ship is not severity. It is the fact that the watch changes at the same hour whether or not anybody feels like it, that the bell is rung, that the same things are done in the same order so that in bad weather nobody has to think about them.
ship.claim: Administrative discipline in an organisation is exactly this: the routine that holds when attention is elsewhere. It is boring by design. That is the point of it.
ship.question: Pick the routine your team most often lets slip when things get busy. That slip is not a symptom of the pressure; it is what turns pressure into failure.

intro: Administrative discipline is the consistent, systematic approach to organising work, maintaining standards, and holding people accountable for results. It creates predictability, reduces chaos, enables efficiency, and allows people to focus on meaningful work. Administrative discipline is liberating — it is not restrictive control but rather the foundation for effective organisations.

blocks.text: Administrative discipline means establishing clear standards, processes, and expectations, then consistently maintaining them across the organisation. Key elements include clear documented processes, consistent application of standards, accountability for results, regular monitoring and follow-up, continuous improvement, proper documentation and records, timeliness, quality standards, resource management, and reliable communication. Why administrative discipline matters:

items: Enables growth: informal systems break down as organisations grow. Discipline creates scalable systems.
Reduces waste: eliminates duplicated work, poor decisions, and resource misallocation.
Improves quality: clear standards and consistent application build reliability and consistency.
Enables accountability: clear expectations make meaningful accountability possible.
Creates predictability: when processes are consistent, people trust and understand the organisation.
Protects knowledge: documented processes preserve organisational knowledge beyond individual people.
Manages risk: systematic approaches identify and manage risks proactively.

blocks.text: The implementation process:

items: Assess the current state: understand what processes exist, what is documented, what is followed consistently, and where chaos exists most.
Communicate why: help people understand that discipline benefits them by creating fairness, efficiency, and predictability — not as restrictive control.
Start with high-impact areas: begin where lack of discipline is causing most problems. Success builds momentum and credibility.
Design and document processes: map current processes, identify inefficiencies, redesign for better flow, and document clearly. Involve staff who perform the work.
Communicate and train: document processes in accessible language, distribute widely, and provide training to ensure understanding.
Monitor and enforce: regularly monitor whether processes are followed, measure performance against standards, provide feedback, and address non-compliance consistently and fairly.
Continuously improve: regularly review processes based on feedback and results data, making adjustments to eliminate inefficiencies and keep processes relevant.

blocks.text: Most organisations require similar core systems. Well-designed, consistently maintained systems create the foundation of administrative discipline.
1. Financial management

Budgeting, accounting practices, expense tracking, financial reporting, controls to prevent fraud, and compliance mechanisms. Without discipline, organisations overspend, lack transparency, cannot track financial status, and risk fraud. With discipline come informed decision-making and stakeholder trust.
2. Human resources management

Consistent hiring, onboarding, job descriptions, performance management, compensation, training, and disciplinary processes. Without discipline, hiring is inconsistent, expectations are vague, and high performers leave. With discipline, the organisation attracts and retains talent, maintains fairness, and develops capabilities.
3. Documentation and records

Organised filing systems, data management, information security, access controls, and retention policies. Without discipline, knowledge is lost, duplicate work occurs, and compliance documentation is missing. With discipline, knowledge is captured, accessible, and protected.
4. Project and workflow management

Project planning, task assignment and tracking, milestone management, resource allocation, quality assurance, and risk management. Without discipline, projects exceed budgets and deadlines. With discipline, projects deliver on time, on budget, with acceptable quality.
5. Quality management

Quality standards, processes designed to maintain standards, monitoring, non-conformance management, and continuous improvement. Without discipline, quality is inconsistent and reputation suffers. With discipline come consistent quality and stakeholder satisfaction.
6. Communication

Defined communication channels, regular meetings, communication norms, information accessibility, and feedback mechanisms. Without discipline, misunderstandings occur and key information does not reach necessary people. With discipline come reliable information flow and organisational alignment.
Obstacle 1: Perception as bureaucratic

People often fear discipline creates bureaucracy that slows things down. In reality, well-designed discipline enables faster decision-making by eliminating waste. Solution: involve people in process design, design processes to be simple and streamlined, frame discipline as enabling innovation, demonstrate time-saving benefits, and build feedback mechanisms for continuous improvement.
Obstacle 2: Resistance from experienced staff

Long-serving employees comfortable with informal systems often resist formal discipline. In reality, informal systems work until organisations grow; then they break down. Discipline protects organisational knowledge and fairness. Solution: involve experienced staff in designing discipline, make them early adopters and champions, show how discipline protects their work, allow transition time, and provide support.
Obstacle 3: Inconsistent enforcement

When some people are held accountable while others are not, credibility erodes. In reality, consistent, fair enforcement is absolutely critical. People accept discipline when it is applied equally. Solution: establish clear expectations, train managers on consistent enforcement, monitor compliance yourself, address inconsistency promptly, document enforcement actions, and make clear that discipline applies to all.
Obstacle 4: Resource constraints

Organisations claim they cannot afford systems when constrained on budget. In reality, struggling organisations most urgently need discipline, because lack of discipline is why they struggle. Investment in discipline returns value quickly through waste elimination and efficiency improvement. Solution: start small with the highest-impact systems, use existing staff, leverage affordable technology, and demonstrate cost savings from reduced waste.

Well-designed discipline actually enables flexibility. The key is building systems that provide structure while allowing adaptation. Core principles for flexibility within discipline: distinguish core processes (critical for consistency) from flexible approaches; build in regular review and adjustment mechanisms; balance standardisation of routine matters with autonomy in creative areas; allow variations appropriate for different contexts; document the “why” not just the “how” so people can adapt thoughtfully; distribute authority for process improvement throughout the organisation; and celebrate adaptive excellence rather than punishing all deviations equally.

blocks.title: building administrative discipline
blocks.text: A humanitarian organisation becomes increasingly chaotic as it grows. Staff complain about unclear expectations and inconsistent treatment. Financial accountability is weak. Quality varies significantly. Leadership decides to implement administrative discipline, starting with financial management and project management (highest impact). They communicate why discipline is needed, work with staff to design improved processes, document procedures, provide training, and begin monitoring compliance — reviewing financial records monthly and project status reports weekly. Within six months, staff report less confusion and greater fairness. Financial records are accurate and enable better decisions. Projects are more organised and deliver better quality. What initially seemed like added bureaucracy becomes appreciated for the clarity and fairness it provides. The organisation has successfully implemented discipline that enables rather than constrains work.

Administrative discipline is the foundation enabling organisations to grow, innovate, serve stakeholders effectively, and create environments where talented people want to work. It is not bureaucracy, control, or rigidity, but rather the systematic foundation for organisational excellence. Leaders who build administrative discipline create stronger organisations that respond effectively to changing circumstances and achieve ambitious goals. The most successful organisations combine ambitious vision and innovation with strong administrative discipline and execution. Organisations with discipline consistently outperform those without it.

tests: Are the core processes in my area documented in a form a new starter could follow?
Is that documentation current, or does it describe how we used to work?
Are standards applied to everyone equally, including me?
Do I monitor compliance, or assume it?
Would our financial records stand up to an audit today?
Could someone else run my area from the documentation if I were away for a month?
Do we know where our records are and who is permitted to access them?
Are our project deadlines met, and if not, do we know why?
Have I involved the people who do the work in designing the process?
Have we changed any process in the last six months because of feedback?
questions: Where does our lack of discipline cost us most?
Which of the four obstacles do we face most strongly?
Is anything we currently call discipline in fact bureaucracy that no longer serves a purpose?
Which of the six essential administrative systems is our weakest?
How do we distinguish core processes from those staff may reasonably adapt?
review.exercise: Pick the process in your area that causes the most confusion. Map it as it actually happens, not as it is supposed to happen. Identify one step that adds no value and remove it.

sections.title: Policy Administration

ship.title: Standing orders
body: A master cannot be on deck at every hour, so the ship carries standing orders: written decisions made in calm weather about what is to be done in circumstances that will recur. They exist so the officer of the watch at three in the morning does not have to invent an answer, and so that two officers do not invent different ones.
ship.claim: A policy that is not written is not a policy — it is a habit that one person happens to hold, and it leaves when they do.
ship.question: Find one decision your team makes repeatedly with no written rule. Someone is guessing, and the guess changes with who is on shift.

intro: Most organisations discover the need for policy the hard way: two people in similar situations are treated differently, someone makes a decision they had no authority to make, or a question that has been answered a dozen times is answered differently on the thirteenth. Policy is the standing answer that prevents this. It is also, in most organisations, the least developed area of administration.

subsections.title: What a Policy Is and Does

blocks.text: A policy is a standing answer to a recurring situation — it saves reasoning a decision from first principles every time it recurs. Every organisation already has policies; the unwritten ones are simply the ones nobody has examined. Writing them down is what makes them reviewable.

blocks.caption: Policy, procedure and directive
head: What it is
Scope
When it ends
rows: A standing decision and the reasoning behind it
When it is withdrawn or revised
The steps by which the policy is carried out
An instruction for one particular situation
When the situation is dealt with

blocks.text: A good policy does five things: states the organisation’s position, delegates safely by fixing the boundaries, gives room for initiative within them, settles foreseeable situations in advance, and creates confidence in decision-making. Policy is usually seen as a constraint on managers; done well, its real effect is to free them.

Trustees make major policy; managers make the rest. You initiate, formulate and keep current the policy that governs your own area, referring upward only what genuinely requires trustee approval. A recurring situation in your area handled inconsistently is a policy gap — and it is yours to close.

Know three things: which policies need trustee approval, what you may approve at your own level, and what to do when no policy covers a live decision. Where these are unclear, managers either escalate everything or approve what they had no authority to approve.

Areas that most often need a written policy: safeguarding, finance and expenditure authority, data protection, recruitment, volunteers, conflicts of interest, complaints, and health and safety. A register and a review cycle keep policies from proliferating, contradicting each other and going stale.

subsections.title: The Five Steps of Policy Administration

blocks.text: Policy administration divides into five stages. Assign each to a named person or role, so that gaps and overlaps become visible.

blocks.caption: The five steps of policy administration
head: Step
What it involves
rows: Establishes the objective, gathers the facts, and drafts an outline before a policy.
Tests it for accuracy, brevity and necessity, takes technical advice, and is given at the right level.
Identifies everyone affected and settles who interprets it and who may authorise an exception.
Issues whatever guidance is needed so that it is applied uniformly.
Reports on where it is and is not being observed, and revises or withdraws it. Two to three years is a reasonable review cycle; where regulation requires more frequent review, follow the regulation.

blocks.text: Whether or not your organisation keeps a formal policy manual, it needs one place where every current policy is recorded with its owner, its approval date and its next review date. The periodic review asks of each policy: is it still being observed? Where is it not, and why? Does it need changing, or does practice? Has it been overtaken by events and should it be withdrawn? A policy nobody can find is not a policy.

One statement many organisations lack governs the relationship between operational teams and support functions. Operational teams direct delivery and are accountable for results; support functions provide the specialist advice, systems and controls within which delivery happens. Neither is subordinate to the other, and neither may act contrary to law, regulation or approved policy. Where this is unwritten, it gets argued about instead.

tests: Could I list the policies that govern my area, and say when each was last reviewed?
Is there a single place where current policies are recorded, and do I know where it is?
Do our documents distinguish policy from procedure, or do they run the two together?
Is there a recurring situation in my area that is handled inconsistently because no policy covers it?
When a policy was last introduced here, was anyone affected consulted before it was approved?
Do I know my own approval limit — which policies I may settle, and which must go to trustees?
Do I know what to do when a decision is needed and no policy covers it?
Do people know who may authorise an exception, and does that person know?
Has anyone checked whether our policies are being interpreted the same way across teams?
Do we know which policies are not being observed in practice, and why?
Is there a policy on our books that has been overtaken by events and should be withdrawn?
Is the relationship between our operational teams and our support functions written down anywhere?
questions: How would we each define a policy, a procedure, a method and a directive? Do our answers match?
Which areas of our work most need a written policy and do not have one?
What are the dangers of writing policies down, and have we experienced any of them?
Who actually initiates policy here — trustees, senior management, or the people doing the work?
What unwritten policies do we operate by — standing answers everyone knows and nobody has recorded?
Where are the opportunities for improving policy in our own organisation?
review.exercise: Identify one situation in your area that recurs and is currently handled by judgement each time. Draft a one-page policy for it, following step one: state the objective, gather the facts, identify who is affected, and name who would need to approve it. Take the draft to your manager. A policy that fits on one page and is actually used is worth more than a manual nobody opens.

sections.title: Management Tools: Documentation and Control

ship.title: The log and the sounding line
body: Two instruments, doing opposite work. The log records where the vessel has been — honest, dated, unarguable. The sounding line tells you the depth under the keel right now, in time to alter course.
ship.claim: Financial records are a log; controls are a sounding line. An organisation with excellent financial records and no controls knows precisely how it ran aground and precisely when — and could have done nothing about it, because everything it measured pointed backwards.
ship.question: Of the figures your team reports monthly, mark which look back and which look forward. Most teams find they have almost no sounding line at all.

intro: Effective management requires more than good intentions and hard work. It requires systematic tools and processes that enable consistent documentation, organisation of information, and coordination across teams and projects. This section presents a practical eight-element documentation management system that can be implemented using Google Drive, Asana, Monday.com, or other modern management platforms. This system provides a scalable approach for organising all projects and organisational units, from small teams to large distributed organisations. Each element serves a specific purpose in the management cycle, and together they create a comprehensive system for planning, executing, monitoring, and learning. The section then turns to management controls — the small set of measures that tell you whether any of it is working.

The system consists of eight key documentation elements that should be maintained for each project, office, or organisational unit. These elements capture the essential information needed for effective management: planning documents, task tracking, meeting documentation, performance reports, event scheduling, financial information, media and communications, and external stakeholder engagement. While all organisations benefit from these elements, each organisation can customise which elements are essential for their context and how they implement them. For example, a large humanitarian organisation might use all eight elements extensively. A small charity might focus on Action Plans, Task Sheets, and Reports. A construction project might emphasise Task Sheets, Meeting Notes, and Reports. The principle remains constant: systematic documentation enables coordination, learning, and accountability.

blocks.text: Purpose: the Action Plan is the strategic document that defines what the project, office, or unit intends to accomplish during a specific period (typically monthly or quarterly). It translates organisational strategy into specific, measurable actions and accountabilities.
Key contents:

items: Strategic objectives: what are we trying to achieve in this period?
Key activities: what major actions will we take?
Responsibilities: who is responsible for each activity?
Timeline: when should each activity be completed?
Success metrics: how will we know if we have succeeded?
Resources required: what resources, budget, or support is needed?
Dependencies: what external factors or other activities must occur for success?
Risk mitigation: what could go wrong and how will we prevent it?

blocks.text: Usage: Action Plans are created monthly for each project or office and reviewed at month-end against actual results. This enables comparison of intended versus actual performance and identification of implementation gaps. Action Plans are the bridge between organisational strategy and daily work.

Purpose: the Task Sheet is the operational document that breaks down action plan activities into specific, manageable tasks. It provides clarity about who is responsible for what, when tasks are due, and current status.
Key contents:

items: Task description: clear description of what needs to be done
Assigned to: who is responsible for completing this task?
Date assigned
Due date: when is the task due?
Current status: Not Started, In Progress, Completed, Cancelled (colour codes: green for completed, blue for cancelled)
Completion date
Priority: High, Medium, Low (colour codes: red for urgent and high priority, yellow for urgent and medium priority, white for low)
Related action plan item: which action plan objective does this task support?
Dependencies: what must happen before this task can be completed?
Notes: any additional information needed to complete the task
Completion evidence: what will demonstrate that the task is actually completed?

blocks.text: Usage: Task Sheets should be reviewed at least weekly — during team meetings or individual check-ins. As tasks are completed, they are marked complete with evidence of completion. This provides transparency about progress and enables early identification of tasks that are blocked or at risk of non-completion.
A Task Sheet template is provided below.

Purpose: Meeting Notes document what was discussed, what decisions were made, and what actions are required. They serve as a record of organisational decisions and create accountability for agreed actions.
Key contents:

items: Meeting date and attendees: when and who participated?
Agenda: what was planned to be discussed?
Key discussions: what was discussed for each agenda item?
Decisions made: what specific decisions were agreed?
Action items: what needs to happen as a result of the meeting?
Responsible person: who is accountable for each action item?
Due date: when is each action item due?
Next meeting: when is the next meeting scheduled?
Distribution list: who needs to receive these notes?

blocks.text: Usage: Meeting Notes should be documented during the meeting (not after), distributed to attendees within 24 hours, and referenced in Task Sheets. Action items from meetings should be tracked in Task Sheets to ensure follow-through. Meeting patterns — what decisions are repeatedly discussed but not resolved — indicate systemic issues requiring attention.

Purpose: Reports provide regular assessment of performance, progress towards goals, challenges encountered, and lessons learned. They enable organisational learning and inform decision-making at higher organisational levels.
Types and key contents:

items: Monthly progress reports: actual results achieved versus action plan objectives, analysis of gaps, challenges encountered, early warning indicators of problems
